name: Hot desert
notes: Widely spaced drought shrubs (creosote, acacias) with columnar and barrel cacti, spiny succulents and ephemeral grasses; Sonoran/Chihuahuan/Mojave with Sahara-Arabian, Namib and Australian variants.

canopy.name: Date palm
canopy.origin: North Africa and the Middle East

growth.juvenile_note: Remote germination: the cotyledon stalk pushes the growing point down into the soil, then grass-like, undivided strap leaves emerge. For several years it is a stemless, spiny fountain of increasingly pinnate, stiff, grey-green fronds, often with suckers (offshoots) at the base, before a rough trunk clad in old leaf bases rises.
growth.source: Wikipedia (to 30 m, slow-growing; fruits 4-8 years after planting, commercial yields at 7-10; offshoots fruit 2-3 years earlier than seedlings; lives 100+ years when maintained); FAO date palm manuals (remote germination, undivided first leaves); height-age estimated from trunk growth

canopy.source: Palm of Sahara, Arabia, Mesopotamia oases; height 15-25 m. Oasis palm; suckers from the base. Standard floras and Kew POWO for the name.

canopy.name: Desert ironwood

growth.juvenile_note: Seeds germinate within days of the summer rains, often under a nurse shrub; the seedling raises two fleshy cotyledons and then small grey-green pinnate leaves with a pair of short curved spines at each node, and drives a deep taproot. It grows slowly into a many-stemmed spiny shrub and, over decades, a broad grey-green tree.
growth.source: Kearney & Peebles, Arizona Flora; Arizona-Sonora Desert Museum, A Natural History of the Sonoran Desert (ironwood: to 10 m, frost-limited, lives several centuries, a nurse tree). Germination, height curve and first seed estimated.

repro.note: bees (carpenter and Centris bees) pollinate; rodents cache the seeds and wash floods carry them

Height to maturity, age at first fruit and lifespan estimated from mesquite literature.

canopy.name: Camel thorn

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal, with two thick oval cotyledons and grey-green feathery bipinnate leaves on a zigzag stem armed with pairs of large, swollen-based, white spines. The seedling pours its effort into a taproot that heads down toward groundwater (in old trees it may reach tens of metres) while the shoot grows slowly, so young plants are sparse, very spiny, grey-green bushes for years.
growth.source: SANBI PlantZAfrica (Vachellia erioloba): 2 m shrub to 16 m tree, slow-growing, starts flowering at about 10 years, seeds take 4-6 weeks to germinate after a boiling-water soak, taproot can reach 60 m; ICRAF Agroforestree: flowers at about 10 yr, regular pod crops by 20 yr, crown to 18 m. Height curve and lifespan estimated.

It soon branches into a low, rounded, silvery-grey mound of stiff, intricately forked twigs, leafy after rains and nearly bare in drought; small spiny burs form among older twigs.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Ambrosia dumosa: large seedling flushes after heavy fall rain (1,151 seedlings/ha after 1976 rains); moist stratification improves 7- and 14-day germination; shrub 20-60 cm, clones to 1 m wide; roots 5-15x stem length, to 70 cm; longevity 'somewhat less than 50 years' (clones perhaps far older); mean flowering May 2. Growth rate and first flowering estimated.

shrub.name: Jumping cholla

growth.juvenile_note: Almost every young plant is a fallen joint or a sterile fruit that rooted where it dropped: a short spiny cylinder that roots from below and puts up a new joint. It thickens into a short dark trunk crowned by whorls of densely spined, silvery-gold jointed branches, and hangs ever-longer chains of green fruits that flower again from the old fruit each summer.
growth.source: Flora of North America vol. 4 (Cylindropuntia fulgida: shrubby to treelike 1-4.5 m; stem segments easily detached; fruits proliferating in long hanging chains, mostly sterile; flowers pink to magenta). Ages and growth estimated from cholla demography.

repro.note: spreads mainly by joints that snag on passing animals and by fallen fruits that root ('sucker' here = rooted joints and fruits); seed is rarely viable

shrub.source: Cylindropuntia fulgida (jumping or chain-fruit cholla), a treelike cholla of the Arizona Upland and Sonoran lowlands, 1-4 m, joints thickly sheathed in silvery-gold spines that detach at a touch, fruits in hanging chains — Flora of North America vol. 4; Kew POWO for the name.

growth.juvenile_note: Seedling: 2 cotyledons, then a few feathery bipinnate true leaves before narrow silvery-grey phyllodes take over in the first months. It sends a taproot ~3 m down while only 20 cm tall and stays a slender silver sprig for years (20 cm at 6-8 months), then becomes a many-stemmed shrub whose branches angle upward like a funnel.

leaf.notes: flat yellow-green lobes 1-3 mm wide, tightly pressed to rock in rosettes 3-10 cm, the centre crowded with small cylindrical isidia; brown-black below

appearance.seasonal: pale yellow-green dry, greener when wet
appearance.refs: Nash et al. 2002 Lichen Flora of the Greater Sonoran Desert Region

ground.name: Desert star moss

growth.juvenile_note: Spores or broken shoots start on soil, rock crevices and the shady foot of boulders and shrubs; short upright shoots crowd into small cushions. Dry, the tongue-shaped leaves twist and curl so the cushion looks dark and shrivelled; wet, they spread into green stars.
growth.source: Flora of North America vol. 27, Syntrichia inermis (small; leaves lingulate, the costa ending at or just beyond the tip, without the long hair-point of S. caninervis; on soil and rock in dry regions). Ages estimated.

repro.note: spores by wind and water and, far more often, broken shoot fragments; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

ground.source: Syntrichia inermis, a small cushion moss of soil, rock and soil crusts in the warm deserts of the American Southwest and Mexico and round the Mediterranean — Flora of North America vol. 27 (Pottiaceae); Tropicos for the name.

traits.native_range: Soil and rock of the warm deserts and the Mediterranean
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

leaf.notes: tongue-shaped leaves 1-3 mm, blunt or with a tiny point, twisted when dry, spreading star-like and green when wet

appearance.seasonal: dark olive-brown and curled dry, green stars after rain
appearance.silhouette: small dark cushions at the foot of rocks

ground.name: Dwarf earthstar

repro.note: The mycelium is the organism and lives in the substrate for years; the fruiting body is what is seen. 'rhizome' here = the mycelium spreading through the substrate; 'wind' = spores.

ground.source: Geastrum schmidelii, a small earthstar of dry sandy soils, dunes and open dry ground; the stalked spore sac has a pleated beak. Records from warm dry regions are fewer than from temperate dunes (estimated fit). Index Fungorum for the name; Sunhede 1989 Geastraceae.

cap.notes: buff to brown rays, often with sand stuck to them

appearance.seasonal: fruits after rain; old stars persist for months

ground.name: Fluffgrass

growth.juvenile_note: A tiny tuft of short, rolled, grey-green blades; its flowering culms bend over and root where the woolly head touches the ground, so one plant becomes a chain of little tufts, each crowned with white fluff.
growth.source: Flora of North America vol. 25 (Dasyochloa pulchella: tufted perennial, often stoloniferous, 3-15 cm; spikelets in dense white-woolly heads among the leaves). Ages estimated.

repro.note: the arching culms root at the head, making chains of tufts

ground.source: Dasyochloa pulchella (syn. Erioneuron pulchellum), a tiny tufted grass of gravelly desert flats and bajadas from California and Utah to Texas and central Mexico, 3-15 cm, crowned with white-woolly spikelets — Flora of North America vol. 25; Kew POWO for the name.

appearance.silhouette: tiny grey tufts tipped with white fluff

ground.name: Sixweeks grama

growth.juvenile_note: Comes up within days of the summer monsoon rains as a tiny tuft of short blades; the culms bend out and root at the nodes into a low spreading patch, flower within about six weeks with little one-sided purplish comb spikes, and die as the soil dries.
growth.source: Flora of North America vol. 25 (Bouteloua barbata: annual, culms 3-30 cm, often decumbent and rooting; 4-11 spikes 1-2.5 cm); the common name records its six-week life after summer rains.

repro.note: a summer ephemeral: seed waits in the soil for the monsoon

ground.source: Bouteloua barbata, an ephemeral summer annual grama of desert flats, washes and roadsides from the SW United States to Mexico and South America, 3-30 cm — Flora of North America vol. 25; Kew POWO for the name.

ground.name: Desert shaggy mane

repro.note: The mycelium is the organism and lives in the substrate for years; the fruiting body is what is seen. 'rhizome' here = the mycelium spreading through the substrate; 'wind' = spores.

ground.source: Podaxis pistillaris (desert shaggy mane), a secotioid fungus of sandy desert soil and termite mounds in the hot deserts of the Americas, Africa, Arabia, India and Australia; the white scaly club-shaped head never opens and fills with dark spores; the young head is eaten in parts of Arabia, Africa and Australia. Index Fungorum for the name; Wikipedia.

cap.form: elongated egg- to club-shaped head 5-15 cm long that never opens, white and shaggy-scaly, splitting with age to show a dark brown-black powdery spore mass
cap.notes: looks like a shaggy inkcap on a stiff stalk; turns brown and papery when old

appearance.habit: solitary or scattered on sand, often from old termite mounds
appearance.seasonal: fruits after rain; dried fruitbodies stand for months
appearance.silhouette: white shaggy clubs standing on bare sand

ground.name: Wavy scaly cloak fern
ground.origin: SW United States to South America
ground.soil_note: A rock-crevice fern: rooted in cracks and ledges of bare rock, never in loose sand or alluvium, so on wash banks it takes the rocky sides, not the sandy floor. pH any: not narrowed to one kind of rock here.

growth.juvenile_note: Spores that lodge in a shaded rock crack grow into a tiny green prothallus during wet spells; the first fronds are small and simple to few-lobed, then come short once-pinnate fronds with a few wavy pinnae. Over several wet seasons the clump builds a tuft of long, narrow, upright fronds wedged in the crack, growing only while it is wet.
growth.source: Spore-to-sporeling time, growth rate and lifespan estimated from fern biology and the genus habit (first fronds simpler than the adult's; growth only after rains); not measured for this species. Adult plant: Kew POWO; Flora of North America vol. 2.

repro.note: spores, no flowers: shed by wind from under the scale layer of fertile fronds; the prothallus grows only in wet spells, so spread reads the rains, not pollinators; compact stem, no clonal spread

ground.source: Astrolepis sinuata (Lag. ex Sw.) D.M.Benham & Windham, wavy scaly cloak fern; long known as Notholaena sinuata (Lag. ex Sw.) Kaulf. and also placed in Cheilanthes, moved to Astrolepis (the star-scaled cloak ferns) by Benham & Windham in 1992. Southwestern United States and Mexico south through Central America into South America, on rocky slopes, ledges and crevices in desert mountains, canyons and dry scrub; tufts of erect, narrow, once-pinnate fronds 20-60 cm, the pinnae shallowly wavy-lobed, grey-green with small star-shaped scales above and densely scaly beneath; the fronds curl and go dull in drought and revive after rain. Temperature, moisture and elevation bands estimated from the range and habitat, not measured. Kew POWO; Flora of North America vol. 2.

traits.native_range: Rocky slopes, ledges and crevices, SW United States to South America
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

leaf.notes: long narrow once-pinnate fronds, a ladder of many small oblong pinnae with shallow wavy lobes; upper side grey-green flecked with tiny pale star-shaped scales, underside hidden under a dense pale tan scale layer that also covers the spores

appearance.seasonal: evergreen; in drought the fronds curl and go dull, and open green again after rain
appearance.silhouette: upright tuft of narrow grey-green ladder fronds in rock cracks
appearance.refs: Kew POWO; Flora of North America vol. 2

ground.silhouette: upright tuft of narrow grey-green ladder fronds in rock cracks

desiccation.source: Astrolepis sinuata: the fronds curl and go dull in drought and revive after rain. Inferred, not measured: the scaly underside showing as the pinnae fold, and every timing - drying set slower than the epiphytic resurrection fern's (a rock crack holds water after rain), revival copied from it. The designer tunes.

ground.name: Spiny cliffbrake
ground.origin: SW United States and northern Mexico
ground.soil_note: A rock-crevice fern: rooted in cracks and ledges of bare rock, never in loose sand or alluvium, so on wash banks it takes the rocky sides, not the sandy floor. pH any: not narrowed to one kind of rock here.

growth.juvenile_note: Spores that lodge in a shaded rock crack grow into a tiny green prothallus during wet spells; the first fronds are small few-lobed blades on thin dark stalks, later ones once and then twice divided. The clump stays compact, adding a few stiff blue-green fronds in each wet season.
growth.source: Spore-to-sporeling time, growth rate and lifespan estimated from fern biology and the genus habit (first fronds simpler than the adult's; growth only after rains); not measured for this species. Adult plant: Kew POWO; Flora of North America vol. 2.

repro.note: spores, no flowers: sporangia along the segment edges under the rolled-under margins, shed by wind; the prothallus grows only in wet spells, so spread reads the rains, not pollinators; compact stem, no clonal spread

ground.source: Pellaea truncata Goodding, spiny cliffbrake: southwestern United States and northern Mexico, on rocky slopes, cliffs and crevices in desert mountains and canyons; compact clumps of stiff fronds 15-45 cm on dark brown, glossy stalks, twice divided into small, narrow, leathery, bluish-green segments with rolled-under edges, each ending in a short sharp tip. Temperature, moisture and elevation bands estimated from the range and habitat, not measured. Kew POWO; Flora of North America vol. 2.
